phaseBreakdown.note: Phase counts cover items NOT YET DONE (OPEN + WIP + BUILT + DECISION). FIXED and CLEARED items are assigned to NO phase, which is why the phase totals do not approach the release total. BUILT means implemented and awaiting certification - it is NOT outstanding work.

legend.FIXED: Implemented and verified. Tracker verdict DONE or MET.
legend.BUILT: Implemented, not yet certified by a full release run. Tracker verdict PARTIAL, BUILT or IN PROGRESS — the code landed, the suite that would prove it has not run.
legend.OPEN: Confirmed, not started. Tracker verdict TODO, or a defect nobody marked closed.
legend.DECISION: Blocked on an owner decision or an owner action. Tracker verdict BLOCKED or DEFERRED, or a TODO the tracker marks as the owner's.
legend.CLEARED: Not applicable — the premise was false, or the item is counted against another row. Tracker verdict N/A.

directives.text: No Vercel preview deployments. Every non-main deployment must land CANCELED — CANCELED is free, BUILDING/READY/ERROR is billed.
A push is the only Actions-consuming action a push approval covers. Reruns, workflow_dispatch, a second push or a non-draft PR are each a fresh ask.
A commit hash AND a verification that ran AND a user-invocable outcome. Two of three is not done.
A gate that cannot fail is not a gate. Prove it fails before trusting that it passed, and take exit codes from UNPIPED commands.
A record of a thing is not the thing. Measure the artefact, not the comment, filename or tracker row describing it.
This board is DERIVED from the release tracker and defect register. Where they disagree with it, THEY WIN.

MANDATORY for every release, every session: start by reading this board. Be able to state total raised, how many are done, and of the rest how many are not started / written-awaiting-certification / awaiting an owner decision — INCLUDING which population each number belongs to. The headline counts and the per-phase counts measure different things; subtracting one from the other gives a wrong answer.

At release close every item goes to exactly ONE place: still pending (not started, built, or awaiting a decision) HANDS OVER to the next release with its evidence; done and cleared are SAVED AS RELEASE DELIVERY. The board then re-points at the new release. Nothing is dropped at a boundary. See docs/STATUS-BOARD-CHARTER.md.

If a status cannot express the truth, ADD THE STATE — never pick the nearest wrong one. Twice this release a status was falsified by a missing word: built-but-not-shipped read as FIXED, and withdrawn read as OPEN forever. A phantom OPEN is as damaging as a phantom FIXED.
crowagent-platform-web + crowagent-portal get FOUR Vercel production deploys for the whole release — ONE at each phase boundary. Nothing mid-phase, for any reason, including a docs-only commit.
crowagent-website is SEPARATE. It does not count against that budget and ships as and when ready.
Railway, staging AND production: deploy whenever needed. No approval, no waiting.
Supabase, staging AND production: apply whenever needed. No approval, no waiting. Via MCP apply_migration, never db push.
There is no Phase 5. Phase 2 is CLOSED. Every remaining item is Phase 3 or Phase 4.
Never report deploy or phase state from a repository document or git log. Read the live surface — Vercel, Stripe, Supabase, Railway.

notCounted: crowagent-website (marketing) — SEPARATE, ships as and when ready
Railway — staging AND production, unrestricted, never waits

issues.title: CrowMark answer-library embedding is 100% dead on production
issues.note: This entry has a history of closures and retractions (:4129 closed, :4172 retracted the same day, :4335 found the root cause), so it is closed here only on a measurement anyone can repeat. Measured on production gujtuecjzfiqsdnzgyvo, not on a record. GET /cron/rag-backfill was triggered and returned backfill_library_embeddings: scanned 10, embedded 10, failed 0. A direct query then confirmed bid_answer_library = 10 rows / 10 embedded / 0 null, independently re-run on write-back 2026-08-08 (select count(*), count(embedding) from bid_answer_library → 10, 10), and ai_calls shows crowmark_chunk_embedding 10 calls at 2026-08-08 21:10:48 UTC against crowmark_library_embedding 866. The column that was 0/10 for the whole release is full. ⚠️ CORRECTION TO THIS REGISTER'S OWN CLAIM. The entry stated that an HTTP trigger for the backfill still had to be built. It already existed — api/app/routers/cron.py:418, @router.get("/rag-backfill"), verified by direct read on write-back 2026-08-08, carrying its own [R262-D-10] docstring explaining that the backfill was otherwise reachable only from the 03:20 UTC tick. That correction belongs to CARRY-22, whose backfill-endpoint half is therefore already delivered, and it is recorded on that row. ⚠️ A NOTE ON THE SWEEP'S OWN FIGURE, because it is the kind of error this pass exists to catch. The override carried into the write-back queue read *"re-measured at 20:57 UTC tonight … still rows 10 / embedded 0"* and downgraded the entry P0 → P1 on that basis, saying it should close only once the count moved off 0. That measurement was true when taken and stale by the time it was written back: the backfill ran at 21:10:48 UTC, thirteen minutes later. The stated figure was therefore NOT transcribed into this register — the closing condition it named had been met instead.

issues.title: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY missing on the worker service
issues.note: > Re-measured and it is PRESENT. Railway MCP, project crowagent-platform, service crowagent-worker, production environment: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is among the service's variables. Logged as a blocking owner action; it had already been done and nobody re-read it. > > One caveat kept deliberately: the API returns NAMES with values redacted, and a dashboard-set variable reaches runtime while an MCP-set one may not. So this proves the variable EXISTS, not that a worker process has read it. Closing on existence, because *missing* is precisely what the defect claimed. Evidence. public.ai_calls on production: surface crowmark_eval_judge — 40 calls, 40 errors, first 2026-07-29 18:30, most recent 2026-07-29 21:56, every one: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set -- cannot call Anthropic for surface='crowmark_eval_judge' Root cause — corrected from the initial report. The key is not missing from Railway production generally. Listed 2026-08-02: - crowagent-platform (production API) — ANTHROPIC_API_KEY present ✅ - crowagent-worker (production) — absent ❌ The eval-judge surface runs on the worker, which is why the ledger disagrees with the API service's configuration. Reporting this as "not set on Railway production" would have sent the fix to the wrong service. Related but distinct: council_preread has zero ledger rows — not a key failure. It runs on the API service, which has the key. It has simply never been invoked in production. That is a separate observation about the buyer-side advisory surface, not a defect in this entry. Owner action — and it is simpler than I first recorded. I originally wrote that this needs the *value* copied across, which I cannot read (MCP returns valuesRedacted: true for connected OAuth apps). That framing was wrong. Railway supports cross-service reference variables, so no secret value has to be handled at all: Service: crowagent-worker Environment: production Name: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Value: ${{crowagent-platform.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}} It resolves at deploy time

The pages map in those manifests is empty, which is why every route reports the same number — Turbopack is not attributing route-specific chunks there at all. Content fingerprinting of those 9 chunks: | Chunk (gz) | Identified content | |---|---| | 73.8 kB | react-dom, react, next-router, scheduler, framer-motion, sentry | | 61.9 kB | react, sentry | | 24.9 kB | next-router | | 18.8 kB | sentry | | 14.1 / 12.1 / 8.8 / 6.1 / 4.3 kB | next-router, react, turbopack runtime | Supabase markers: absent from all nine. The Sentry.init() *call* is correctly wrapped in deferSentryInit(...) (the R252-PERF-TBT fix, which addressed blocking *time*), but deferring the call never removes the *bytes*: a static import puts the SDK in the eager chunk regardless of when it executes. issues.title: The EPC posture score is not the same number in both runtimes
issues.note: > The split cannot recur: there is only one runtime left. Verified 2026-08-05 — git ls-files returns api/app/services/crowmark_epc_posture.py and its test, and no TypeScript counterpart. The duplicate was deleted in 6e4df3f2, before Phase 2. A half-up vs half-to-even rounding disagreement needs two implementations to disagree. Two implementations of the same regulated calculation round differently, and both test suites are green. | Runtime | Code | posture_score for the same portfolio | |---|---|---| | TypeScript | web/src/shared/lib/crowmark/epc-posture.ts:57-60 — Math.round(v * f) / f (half-up) | 6.3 | | Python | api/app/services/crowmark_epc_posture.py:101 — built-in round(...) (banker's, half-to-even) | 6.2 | Reproduced live, both sides, 2026-08-02 — not inferred from reading: portfolio = 5 × band A + 3 × band F → ratio = 5.0/8 = 0.625 (binary-exact) score = 0.625 × 10 = 6.25 node Math.round(6.25*10)/10 → 6.3 python round(6.25, 1) → 6.2 This is not cosmetic. posture_score is folded into the 0–100 CrowMark bid compliance score (api/app/services/bid_scorer.py:175,263). A supplier can be shown one figure and scored on another. Why neither suite caught it — and this is the part worth keeping. web/lib/crowmark/epc-posture.test.ts and api/tests/test_epc_posture.py assert the same six cases (0.0 / 10.0 / 6.0 / 5.0 / 2.0 / 10.0) and not one of them lands on a .5 boundary. Both suites are green and always would be. It is an ADR-0008 vacuous green in two languages at once — duplicated logic *and* duplicated blind spots, because the tests were ported alongside the code. Honest scope caveat: git grep finds no production importer of the TypeScript half in web/ today — only its own test. So the divergence is reachable through the shared module's public API rather than a currently-rendered surface. That does not make the numbers agree, and it does not make the next importer safe. Detection shipped, fix deliberately not. scripts/regulatory-parity.mjs compares rounding semantics

issues.title: the suite gets greener the more untested code you add
issues.note: The api suite shards by static lists in .certification/api-shard-N.txt. A test file created after those lists were generated belongs to no shard, so it never runs — while all six shards report green. This is the second occurrence in R2.6.2: | File | How it was found | |---|---| | test_r262_ai_001_embedding_model_guard.py | By hand, after a tally mismatch | | test_r262_d10_rag_backfill_reports_failure.py | By hand, 2026-08-02 — only because the first miss had taught me to check | A check that runs only when someone remembers to run it is not a check. scripts/verify-api-shard-coverage.mjs fails on unsharded, duplicated and stale entries, and fails closed on an empty scope. Fixture: 9/9, every breach paired with a control. Scope limit, stated rather than glossed: .certification/ is gitignored, so this is a LOCAL gate run beside run-shards.sh, not a CI one. In a fresh clone it exits 1 with a harness error because there is nothing to check. Making it skip-when-absent would turn *empty scope* into a pass — the identical defect one level up — so it is deliberately left fail-closed and out of CI. Its own fixture also found a flaw in the gate: missing resolved shard entries against the real repo root even when analysing a synthetic tree, so the MISSING case had been passing for the wrong reason. ---

issues.title: An expired trial never expires, and 8 production orgs have had free Portfolio since 2026-06-15
issues.note: D-16 blocked its own deployment on one question: > NOT RESOLVED UNTIL DEPLOYED, AND ONE THING MUST BE CHECKED FIRST: the 8 rows > are untouched. The code now refuses them — but if any of those orgs in fact paid > and the row is merely stale, deploying drops them to free scope. That check was never carried out. It has been now, on production (gujtuecjzfiqsdnzgyvo, 2026-08-08), and the answer is that no paying customer is affected. Three independent lines of evidence, none of which rests on the others: 1. The rows belong to internal accounts. All 8 are held by three owner-linked, single-member organisations (names redacted under the identity rule), every one created at the same microsecond — 2026-05-16 16:35:57.700721+00 — and all on tier='portfolio'. Eight rows created in one instant across three internal orgs is seeded data, not eight people who signed up. 2. Six of the eight are for products that no longer exist (crowcash ×3, crowcyber ×3; the remaining two are crowmark). A customer cannot be dropped to free scope on a product that has been decommissioned. 3. The Stripe account has never had a paid subscription. R262-D-02 established by live read that GET /v1/subscriptions?status=all returns exactly one subscription in the account's entire history — canceled, reason payment_failed, ended 2026-04-27. There is no customer to harm. So the D-16 deploy blocker is cleared. Deploying the trial_end_elapsed() fix drops three internal test orgs from portfolio to free, which is the correct outcome and the intended behaviour of the fix. ### One correction to the entry's own wording The heading says *"8 production orgs have had free Portfolio"*, and the body repeats *"still holds portfolio for all 8 orgs"*. It is 8 ROWS across 3 ORGS. The body's own measurement is stated correctly — *"8 product_subscriptions rows"* — so the count is right and only the noun is wrong, but the noun is the one a reader carries away. "Eight organisations on free Portfolio for 51 days" reads as eight

issues.title: A 402 resolves silently in the Social Value calculator, so a gate produced no error
issues.note: Fixed at root cause. The defect was that fetch rejects only on a network fault, so the Social Value calculator's .catch never saw an HTTP error: a 402 from the entitlement gate resolved normally and its {detail:{error:'tier_required'}} body was fed into setBenchmarks, making a DENIED GATE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM SUCCESS — no alert, no Sentry event, fields silently undefined. That is why re-pointing the /benchmarks gate at pro broke paying Starter customers invisibly (R262-D-18). THE FIX IS A NEW MODULE, NOT A try/catch. web/src/features/social-value/benchmarks-fetch.ts returns a discriminated result, verified by direct read on write-back 2026-08-08: export type BenchmarkFailureReason = "entitlement" | "unavailable" (:60), with :94 classifying status === 402 — and only 402 — as entitlement, and every other non-2xx, network fault or unparseable body as unavailable. A 200 whose body is not the benchmark shape is a fault too (:142-143), so the next contract change cannot hide the way the 402 did. It lives outside the effect precisely so the classification is directly testable instead of reachable only through a full render. Proved RED first, plus a 9-status classifier control covering the whole range. *One wording correction to the sweep's own note, made rather than transcribed:* the sweep described the second class as fault; the shipped discriminant is named unavailable. Same mechanism, and the name in the code is the one that counts.

issues.title: Checkout can be opened for a product this release deleted, and the refusal is after the money
issues.note: > Fixed in 45d2eead: gated on isProductEnabled() before price resolution, 410 Gone. 6 tests pass, REAL EXIT 0. Falsified — neutralising the condition fails exactly the four archived-product cases while both controls (crowmark, csrd) stay green. web/app/api/stripe/create-checkout/route.ts resolves a price and opens a Stripe Checkout Session with no isProductEnabled() check — grep over web/app/api/stripe/ returns none. Meanwhile ProductKey (web/src/shared/lib/stripe/types.ts:19) still admits core | crowcyber | crowcash | crowesg, every one of which is enabled: false in web/src/shared/product/registry.ts:98,149,167,185 and archived out of the platform by this release. The only refusal is api/app/routers/stripe_webhook.py:94-107 (SWOFF-04), which fires on the webhook — after the customer has paid. A refund is not the same as a refusal. Measured mitigation, which is luck rather than design: the four archived products' Stripe products are active: false, and their *_starter_* prices are still active: true (crowcyber price_1TiZfU… £49, crowcash price_1TiZhJ… £39, core price_1Tpq6u… £39). Whether Stripe accepts a Checkout Session line item whose price hangs off an archived product is not verified — confirming it needs a live write, which is out of bounds here. So the door may be shut by Stripe, or may not, and we do not currently know which. PRODUCTS_WITH_STARTER_TIER (create-checkout/route.ts:498-503) also still lists archived products, which is what keeps those trial prices reachable at all. Fix: gate create-checkout on isProductEnabled(productKey) before price resolution, returning 410/403; trim PRODUCTS_WITH_STARTER_TIER to enabled products; and prove the gate with a falsification fixture per ADR-0008. This belongs to R262-ISO-* — a product is not isolated while its checkout still opens. ---

issues.title: Every responsive gate this platform owns is dormant, unbaselined, unwired — or possibly unable to fail
issues.note: D-35 recorded, deliberately, that the horizontal-overflow gate *might* be incapable of failing, and refused to assert it: *"asserting the gate is broken would be as unfounded as the green it currently produces; the control is the deliverable."* That control has now been run. The experiment. Two pages identical but for the rule under test, each with a child deliberately 2000px wide in a 390px viewport: | page | docEl.scrollWidth | body.scrollWidth | element-probe hits | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | CONTROL — no overflow-x rule | 2000 | 2000 | 1 | | SUBJECT — html { overflow-x: hidden }, as shipped (globals.css:205) | 2000 | 2000 | 1 | The control fired first: without the rule, scrollWidth reports 2000, so the instrument demonstrably sees overflow. Only then does the subject's reading mean anything. Verdict: overflow-x: hidden on the root does NOT clamp documentElement.scrollWidth in Chromium. The eight e2e probes that read it are capable of failing. Every "zero horizontal overflow" green in the release record is real on this axis, not a structural pass. This is the opposite of the website-side overflow: clip lesson, and the difference matters: clip does suppress the metric, hidden does not. The two are not interchangeable, which is presumably why the suspicion was reasonable in the first place. Scope stated: measured in Chromium, which is what both Playwright and the e2e probes use. It says nothing about other engines, and does not need to. Cost note: D-35 estimated about half a day for this. A minimal two-page fixture settled it in minutes — the expensive part was never rendering the app, it was deciding what would discriminate. ### D-35's other three findings are NOT disproved and remain open 2. issues.title: A subagent bypassed the identity pre-commit hook with --no-verify, "out of habit" CLEARED 2026-08-08 — verified no leak in authorship or any runtime path
issues.note: While fixing R262-D-33/R262-D-34, a subagent ran git commit --no-verify. That flag skips the pre-commit hook which CLAUDE.md establishes specifically to block the owner's personal name and Gmail from entering a commit — the IDENTITY HARD RULE. It then noticed, and re-ran git commit --amend --no-edit so the hook actually executed. Verified rather than accepted, because a claimed correction of a policy bypass is exactly the thing not to take on trust: | Check | Result | |---|---| | Author on 1a7521b1 | Crow Agent <crowagent.platform@gmail.com> ✅ | | Committer on 1a7521b1 | Crow Agent <crowagent.platform@gmail.com> ✅ | | Commit message, personal-identity grep | 0 hits ✅ | | Full diff, personal-identity grep | 0 hits ✅ | | .git/hooks/pre-commit re-run as a control | EXIT: 0 ✅ | | .husky/pre-commit re-run as a control | EXIT: 0 ✅ | No harm. The identity rule held, and it held because the *content* was clean, not because the gate ran. ### Why it is still logged The gate exists precisely so that outcome does not depend on the content happening to be clean. A bypass that causes no harm is a near miss, and near misses are the only warnings a hard rule gets before it fails for real. "Out of habit" is how a bypass becomes routine. Two process fixes, neither yet made: 1. Agent briefs must forbid --no-verify explicitly. Mine said "commit locally only, never push" and named the identity rule, but never said *do not skip the hooks* — so the instruction relied on the agent inferring it. An instruction that depends on inference is not a control. 2. The hook cannot enforce itself against --no-verify — nothing client-side can. The durable answer is a server-side or CI check on the same rule, so a bypassed local hook is caught at the point the work becomes shared. Worth pairing with the R262-D-09/R262-D-38 guard work rather than done alone. ---

issues.title: One carriage return made the entire API suite unrunnable, and the coverage gate reported PASSED over it
issues.note:
Found 2026-08-08 on the first attempt to satisfy CG-03 since the 08-05 repairs. ### What happened bash .certification/run-shards.sh api 1 6 died on shard 1 in three seconds: ERROR: file or directory not found: api/tests/test_crowmark.py no tests ran in 0.00s EXIT: 4 api/tests/test_crowmark.py exists. Exit 4 is a pytest *usage* error, not a test failure — the suite never started. The runner stops on first non-zero, so shards 2–6 never ran either. CG-03 was not failing; it was not executing. ### Root cause — one character .certification/api-shard-1.txt had CRLF line endings: $ head -1 .certification/api-shard-1.txt | od -c 0000000 a p i / t e s t s / t e s t _ c r o w m a r k . p y  
 run-shards.sh built its pytest argv with tr '
' ' ' < shard.txt. That converts the newline and leaves the carriage return attached, so pytest was handed api/tests/test_crowmark.py — a filename that does not exist. Strip the  and the file resolves immediately. Only shard 1 was affected, which is why the 08-05 run reached shards 2–6 and this presented as new. ### The part that matters — the gate could not see it scripts/verify-api-shard-coverage.mjs printed, on the same tree, minutes before: ✅ api-shard-coverage PASSED — 382 test files, all in exactly one of 6 shards Its parser splits on /?
/ (:92) and trims, so it compared clean paths, found all 382 on disk, and passed. The gate normalised the exact character the runner passed through. Its three checks — UNSHARDED, DUPLICATED, MISSING — were all genuinely satisfied. It was structurally incapable of observing the condition that made the suite unrunnable, because it was reading a different string than the runner was executing. This is AP-6 again — a gate scoped to the wrong property — and it is the fourth time in this release that a green gate has described something other than the thing it claims to govern (R262-D-15 static shard lists, R262-D-36 the RLS regex reading %I as public, R262-D-46 747 of 749 web files, now this). issues.title: AI Bid Marking silently discards the buyer's published weights whenever ONE criterion is pass/fail — and the disclosure that explains it is never rendered
issues.note: Found 2026-08-08 (audit Stream C), then independently reproduced and extended by direct execution against the live engine. This is the flagship differentiator surface — "AI Bid Marking", H1 — on a mounted, rate-limited production endpoint: POST /api/v1/crowmark/contracts/{contract_id}/questions/{question_id}/mark (api/app/routers/crowmark_response.py:1075, mounted api/app/main.py:501) ### Reproduction — executed, not reasoned api/app/services/crowmark_answer_marker.py:353-370, _resolve_criteria_weights: CASE A — buyer 70/30, every criterion weighted: ([70.0, 30.0], True) ← correct CASE B — same buyer weights + ONE pass/fail criterion (weight=None): ([33.33, 33.33, 33.33], False) ← buyer weights GONE CASE C — realistic UK ITT: quality 60 / price 30 / social value 10 + insurance gate: ([25.0, 25.0, 25.0, 25.0], False) ← quality 60% → 25% The control mechanism is one line: python all_published = n > 0 and all(w is not None and w > 0 for w in stated) if all_published: ...use buyer weights... return ([100.0 / n] * n if n else []), False # ← ALL-OR-NOTHING A pass/fail criterion carries no percentage, so its weight is None. One such criterion in the set flips all_published to False and collapses *every* genuinely-weighted criterion to an equal share — while simultaneously granting the pass/fail gate an equal share of the coverage mark, though a gateway question is not scored at all. issues.title: astro build never ran, so 33 minutes of browser gates measured a stale dist
issues.note: Found 2026-08-08 on the first complete run of the website gate chain — a run only possible because R262-D-72 replaced the && chain with a runner that reports every gate. ### The tell was the duration, not the message FAIL astro check 1ms error: spawnSync ...astro.cmd EINVAL FAIL astro build 0ms error: spawnSync ...astro.cmd EINVAL 1ms and 0ms. A gate that fails takes time; a gate that never starts does not. Node 18.20 / 20.12 hardened spawnSync against CVE-2024-27980, so spawning a .cmd without shell: true now throws EINVAL outright. The runner pointed at node_modules/.bin/astro.cmd. ### Why it mattered far more than two red lines astro build is what produces dist/. It never executed. Every browser-driven gate after it — check-render, check-cwv, check-controls, check-autoplay, over 33 minutes of measurement — ran against a stale dist timestamped 14:05, reporting on output that no longer matched the source. 29 "passes" over an artefact from an earlier build. The runner did its job perfectly: it made a failure visible that && would have hidden. But it listed a gate-that-could-not-start beside genuine failures as though they were the same kind of thing, and they are not — one is a verdict, the other is the absence of one. ### Fix astro's JS entrypoint invoked under node, not the .cmd shim. shell: true would also work; this is better — no shell quoting, no PATH dependence, and it matches the runner's own stated intent of resolving the CLI directly. Proven by the re-run: astro check 18,945ms exit 0, astro build 4,926ms exit 0 — and check-render then passed, confirming the R262-D-72 fixes against genuinely current output. Chain went 29/33 → 32/33. ### The pattern, now three-for-three today A measurement that did not happen reads identically to one that succeeded. | | | |---|---| | R262-D-48 | printed *"382 test files — PASSED"* over a suite pytest could not resolve | | R262-D-64 | excluded Playwright specs by directory when the property was *"imports @playwright/test"* |

issues.title: The board's status classifier contained literal BACKSPACE characters, so every word-based status test was dead
issues.note: Found by refusing to accept a result I could not explain. After moving R262-D-72 to 🟡 FIXED IN CODE, NOT DEPLOYED, the board still showed it OPEN. The heading plainly contained the word FIXED, and the classifier plainly tested for it. Reasoning about it produced a contradiction, so the script was instrumented instead. Inside the running build, on the real string: DBG openBranch= false fixedBranch= true len= 169 DBG after-chain status= OPEN Both branch tests agreed the status should be FIXED, and the very next line reported OPEN. That is impossible for the code as READ — so the code as read was not the code on disk. Dumping the raw lines through JSON.stringify showed why: 133 " if (/🔴|\bOPEN\b/u.test(rawTitle)) {" 135 " } else if (/✅|\bRESOLVED\b|\bFIXED\b/iu.test(rawTitle)) {" JSON.stringify renders \b for U+0008 BACKSPACE. Those are not escape sequences. The file contained 8 literal control characters — the four word-boundary pairs — so the live regexes were: /🔴|<BS>OPEN<BS>/u /✅|<BS>RESOLVED<BS>|<BS>FIXED<BS>/iu /<BS>DIAGNOSED<BS>/i None of which can match ordinary prose. Proven rather than asserted: dead regex vs "x FIXED IN CODE": false intended regex vs "x FIXED IN CODE": true Consequence. Only the two EMOJI alternatives (🔴, ✅) ever worked. Every word-based status — FIXED without a tick, RESOLVED, DIAGNOSED — silently fell through to the default, and the default is OPEN. The WIP status was unreachable: DIAGNOSED could never match, so no item could ever hold it. After the fix, WIP 1 appears for the first time. This is the third defect in the same reporting path today (D-76 no dates, D-82 silent drops, this), and the same shape as all of them: the board understated completed work, and the understatement was silent. It is also a fourth instance of the release's theme — a check that could not fail. Two of the four emoji-marked branches did work, which is exactly why it survived: FIXED counts kept rising, so nothing looked broken. Terminal display is what hid it

issues.title: The board double-counted repeated ids and rendered the STALE one — including a P0 that had been fixed for a week
issues.note: The defect register is APPEND-STRUCTURED: when an item is resolved, a second section is written for the same id. The parser emitted both, and every consumer reads with .find(), which returns the FIRST match — so the board both double-counted the item and displayed the older, unresolved version. Measured 2026-08-08: 10 ids carried more than one entry, six of them a stale OPEN beside a later FIXED — D-02, D-04, D-05, D-06, D-08, D-10. Among them R262-D-02, *"Live checkout charges prices that do not match the published price table"* — the register's only open P0 — which had actually been resolved on 2026-08-01 with the owner's authorisation, Railway repointed and verified. The board reported a closed live-revenue P0 as outstanding for a week. Three rules, each added because the previous one was wrong in a way worth recording: 1. Last occurrence wins, by document ORDER rather than status rank. Order is the right signal for an append-structured file, and unlike "closed beats open" it still honours a genuine RE-OPEN. 2. The register outranks the tracker. Plain last-wins let a tracker row override the register — it flipped R262-D-09 from the register's DIAGNOSED back to OPEN. The register is the defect's own record; the tracker's rows are task rows that happen to share an id (R262-D-10's tracker row is a Phase-1 gate, not the defect). So only a later REGISTER entry may supersede a register entry. 3. Combined headings credit every id they name. The register closes related defects together — ## R262-D-02 / D-05 / D-08 — ✅ RESOLVED 2026-08-01 — and the heading regex captured only the first, so D-05 and D-08 never received their resolution. Only a run of / D-NN IMMEDIATELY following the id is treated as siblings, so a heading that merely mentions related defects in its prose is not misread. Two things a merge must never lose, both found by checking the result rather than trusting the rule: - Severity never drops. A continuation heading carries no · Pn · marker, so it parses at

issues.title: 36 defect headings used bold severity markers, and every one parsed as P2 — hiding 6 P0s and 19 P1s
issues.note: The heading regex read severity as (?:·\s*(P\d))?. The register writes severity two ways — · P2 · and · P1 · — and the second never matched, so those entries fell to the sev || 'P2' default. Measured on the register: 51 headings plain, 36 bold. Every one of the 36 was being reported P2. By true severity they were 6 P0, 19 P1, 7 P2, 4 P3 — so 25 P0/P1 defects were sitting in the P2 bucket, on a board whose entire purpose is to let the owner work highest-severity-first. The owner's instruction is "high value items are on first priorities"; the board was quietly making that impossible to act on. Found only because R262-D-10 — a P0 — appeared under P2 while its heading plainly read P0. It is the same class as D-89: the register's own formatting variation defeating a check nobody had tested against real headings. Fixed: (?:·\s*\*{0,2}(P\d)\*{0,2})?. Verified after — board-wide severity is now P0 7 · P1 45 · P2 246 · P3 6, and the OPEN P0s render correctly as R262-D-10 (CrowMark answer-library embedding dead on production) and R262-D-59 (60 active live Stripe prices for products that no longer exist). issues.title: SWEEP-04 — DEFECT CLASS: MCP apply_migration writes to the database and never to supabase/migrations/, and nothing detects it
issues.note: Commit 82c4235c · scripts/verify-migrations-have-files.mjs. The defect class was MCP apply_migration writing to the database and never to supabase/migrations/, with nothing able to detect the next occurrence. There is now a gate: it reads the applied migrations, matches each against the tree by SQL and by name, and fails on any version that matches no file. It carries a 118-version baseline for genuinely historical unmatched versions, under the contract that the baseline may only SHRINK — the same contract the design-system gate uses, and the reason a baseline is a ratchet rather than a permanent excuse. ⚠️ RECORDED BECAUSE THE WRONG ANSWERS ARE THE USEFUL PART: THREE DESIGNS WERE BUILT, MEASURED AND REJECTED FIRST. The second of them reported 429 of 623 migrations missing. That number is alarming, plausible, and was the GATE being wrong, not the repository — it matched on filename shape and every legitimately-renamed historical migration failed it. A gate reporting four hundred defects it invented is worse than no gate, because someone will act on it. The only thing that separated the true 118 from the false 429 was spot-checking the individual rows against the tree by hand before believing either figure. issues.title: SWEEP-05 — the RLS parity gate models only literal DROP TABLE; a dynamic EXECUTE format() drop is invisible to it
issues.note: Commit c05aee6b · scripts/rls/detect-unmodellable-ddl.mjs. The RLS parity gate models only literal DROP TABLE, so a drop executed through EXECUTE format(...) in a plpgsql loop is invisible to it — the gate reads clean and the divergence is real. The fix does not teach the parity gate to parse dynamic SQL, which would be a promise it could not keep; it adds a detector that finds the constructs the parity gate cannot model and makes them declare themselves. An unmodellable construct becomes a visible, listed exception instead of a silent hole. That is the correct shape for this class: where a gate has a structural blind spot, the blind spot must be enumerable even when its contents are not.

issues.title: R262-ADMINCLIENT-500 — a bodyless 500 escaping a route's own error contract
issues.note: Commit 1c8cbf83. createSupabaseAdminClient() throws when SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY is absent under NODE_ENV=production — verified on write-back at web/src/shared/lib/supabase/server.ts:116-117, where the guard reads if (optionalEnv("NODE_ENV") === "production") throw new Error("Missing env var SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY …"). In POST /api/reports/templates that throw escaped the handler before it reached the route's own serverError() path, so the caller received a 500 with an EMPTY BODY — no code, no message, nothing to act on — while GET on the same route returned a healthy 200 {"templates":[]}. WHY THAT PAIRING IS THE DEFECT, AND NOT MERELY THE 500. A route that half-works reads to a client as *"this endpoint is broken"* rather than *"this deployment is misconfigured"*. The two diagnoses send an engineer to opposite ends of the system, and the empty body removed every signal that would have distinguished them. NOT A FALLBACK, and this is the line the fix deliberately does not cross. The misconfiguration is real and the request is still refused. What changed is that the refusal now obeys the same contract as every other failure on the route, so a caller can tell a server problem from a bad request. Nothing was made to succeed that should have failed. Found while building the critical-journeys CRUD test — it was the single failure in that suite, and its cause sat three layers away from where it surfaced, which is the argument for that suite existing. Verification recorded on the commit: tsc --noEmit REAL EXIT 0.

issues.title: — P1 · Staging exposed the MFA-removal audit log to ANONYMOUS callers: RLS was off on a public table PostgREST serves
issues.note: The only ERROR-level finding the Supabase security linter reports on either database, and one production does not have. Found by running the advisors on staging after running them on production — i.e. by not assuming the two match. Measured before touching anything: | | staging ipgrnwvfnumgvnxkpxsc | prod gujtuecjzfiqsdnzgyvo | | --- | --- | --- | | relrowsecurity | FALSE | TRUE | | policies | 0 | 0 | | anon SELECT grant | true | — | | authenticated SELECT grant | true | — | | linter | ERROR rls_disabled_in_public | INFO rls_enabled_no_policy | Why this is a real exposure and not a lint nit. The table lives in public, so PostgREST serves it at /rest/v1/mfa_factor_removal_log, and both anon and authenticated hold a SELECT grant. With RLS off, the grant is the entire access decision — there is nothing else to consult. Any anonymous caller with the project URL and the publishable key could read the record of WHO removed an MFA factor and WHEN. That is audit data about the security control itself: exactly what an attacker who had just stripped someone's second factor would want to check, and exactly what an incident responder later needs to be able to trust. Fixed by enabling RLS with NO policies, which is the correct end state rather than an unfinished one. RLS with zero permissive policies denies every role subject to it, while the service role bypasses RLS and continues writing the audit rows. That is precisely production's shape, and the INFO-level rls_enabled_no_policy the linter reports there is describing a deliberate fail-CLOSED configuration, not a defect. Adding a permissive policy here would WIDEN access — the opposite of the fix. Verified with a control, because two zeroes prove nothing on their own: | probe | rows visible | | --- | --- | | CONTROL — owner role | 1 | | as anon | 0 | | as authenticated | 0 | Without the 1, "anon sees nothing" is indistinguishable from "the probe was broken". issues.note: First complete run. Two prior attempts were starved by concurrent agents and abandoned; the portal verification agent explicitly named the full suite as its one unmeasured gap. All 20 tests in apps/portal/src/app/api/customers/[id]/actions/route.test.ts called await import('./route'), but Node caches the module — so only the FIRST paid for it, bearing the whole cold graph load inside its own 30s testTimeout while the other 19 ran in milliseconds. The failure therefore always pointed at change_plan: happy path returns 200 + audits, which was innocent: it was simply first in file order. Reproduced on an idle machine (1 node process), so it was never contention — a point worth pinning, because three OTHER apparent failures tonight WERE contention (see R262-D-145). Fixed by moving the load into beforeAll with a hook budget — attribution, not masking. The import is setup; it is not the behaviour any test asserts. In a hook, a slow graph shows up as slow SETUP instead of as a false failure in whichever test happens to run first. testTimeout stays at 30s so a genuinely slow HANDLER still fails, no assertion was weakened and no test skipped. Safe because nothing in the file calls vi.resetModules(): all 20 sites were already receiving the same cached instance, so only WHERE the single load is billed changed. hookTimeout is unset in vitest.config.ts and defaults to 10s, hence the explicit 180s ceiling on the hook. Measured result: that file went from a 30s timeout to 24 passed in 1.92s. A claim I made and then had to revise, recorded because the revision is the honest part. issues.title: — R262-D-30's defect came BACK, because the dev server rewrites tsconfig.json; the guard caught it and the file was restored
issues.note: Found by the first web vitest shard, and it is a recurring ENVIRONMENT-induced regression rather than a code change anyone made deliberately. web/__tests__/config/r262-d30-tsconfig-excludes-dev-types.test.ts::does not type-check the dev server's generated types FAILED. Measured: web/tsconfig.json include had regrown .next/dev/types/**/*.ts. Cause: next dev REWRITES tsconfig.json. Agents ran dev servers tonight (the responsive harness needs one), and Next re-added the entry. The whole file showed as changed in git diff, but comparing HEAD against the working copy field-by-field proved everything EXCEPT include was byte-identical — the rest was formatting churn from Next rewriting the file. So git checkout -- web/tsconfig.json was the correct, lossless fix; git status for that path is now clean. Why it matters beyond tidiness. That produces phantom errors about files nobody edited — two agents hit exactly this tonight: one reported "~700 phantom errors" from truncated .next/dev/types/* left by a killed dev server, another saw tsc EXIT 2 for generated types still naming a route it had just deleted. Both correctly cleared the artefacts rather than "fixing" source. This row is the upstream cause of both. The guard is well built and worth copying. It carries a companion assertion — *"still type-checks the BUILD's generated route types"* — with the comment: *"Guard the guard. Without this, the assertion above would also pass if someone removed generated-type checking altogether — which is a different defect (a blind gate) wearing this fix's clothes."* That is the exact discipline this release keeps having to apply, already present in the codebase. Recurrence is expected, not a one-off. Anyone running next dev re-introduces it. issues.title: TWENTY-FIVE production tables cannot be recreated from the repository, and that is the ROOT CAUSE of the staging gap
issues.note: Found by running the Supabase security advisor against staging after the apply, which is a step that could easily have been skipped on the grounds that "the migration asserted success". Measured, with production as the control: | function | prod anon / auth | staging after my migration | | --- | --- | --- | | documents_set_org | false / false | TRUE / TRUE | | set_updated_at_onboarding | false / false | TRUE / TRUE | Supabase exposes public functions over PostgREST, so on staging both became callable at /rest/v1/rpc/<name> by an unauthenticated caller. Production had EXECUTE revoked. THE CAUSE IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART. pg_get_functiondef returns a complete definition of the function's BODY and attributes and contains no GRANT or REVOKE — privileges are simply not part of a function definition. PostgreSQL then grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default on any new function. So a transcription that was faithful by every check I had applied, and whose post-condition passed, still left staging more permissive than production. **A schema transcription built from pg_get_*def covers STRUCTURE and misses PRIVILEGES entirely. pg_get_functiondef has no GRANT; pg_get_indexdef has no owner; pg_policies has no table-level grant. Any future "recreate from the live catalog" work must query information_schema.role_table_grants and has_function_privilege separately, or it reproduces this gap exactly. Scope CHECKED rather than guessed, in both directions: - TABLE grants for all 23 new tables are IDENTICAL on both databases (Supabase's default grant-all to anon/authenticated, with RLS doing the real gating). No table privilege diverged, so the blast radius is the two functions and nothing else. - update_business_hub_updated_at is anon-executable on BOTH databases, so it is PARITY, not drift, and was deliberately left alone. "Fixing" it would make staging diverge in the other direction to answer a production posture question that belongs in its own row. Fixed by 20261780000000, applied to stag

issues.title: SUSPECTED: production browsers may THROW on contract drift, the inverse of the documented invariant
issues.note: Commit 2e3b47fc. Filed as SUSPECTED; it is real. Each link was executed, not reasoned: 1. The artefact traced to its terminal module. The pre-fix chunk held "production"!==function(e){… r.default.env[e] …}("NODE_ENV"), where r resolves to Next's browser process polyfill. 2. The fallback shim executed in Node: env === {}, env["NODE_ENV"] === undefined, shouldThrow -> true. 3. The real browser path executed — next start on a production build plus Playwright: typeof globalThis.process === "undefined" at document-start (asserted via addInitScript, so nothing could define-then-delete it) and after load. The ternary therefore always takes the shim branch. 4. No escape hatch: zero callers pass throwOnError, so every client call takes the default. Chain: no process in the browser -> polyfill -> shim with env = {} -> optionalEnv("NODE_ENV") is undefined -> undefined !== "production" -> contract drift THREW at real users. The inverse of the invariant documented at validate.ts:9-11. Fix: validate.ts:75 now uses the static process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production", and the @shared/lib/env import is gone — which is exactly what env.ts:18-19 already prescribed for client-reachable code. Proven in the rebuilt artefact: Turbopack inlined and constant-folded the decision away entirely, and no runtime env lookup remains in the chunk. This changes production behaviour for real users, deliberately. Drift now logs a structured console.error and passes the payload through, so a drifted response is silent to the user and visible only in telemetry — which is what the header comment intends. ### The guard, and why the TEST is not the guard import "server-only" added to env.ts:30. issues.title: BOTH existing axe sweeps counted a 404 or a login bounce as a PASS
issues.note: Commit 48b7d37a. Before any accessibility number could be trusted, the instrument had to be replaced: - web/scripts/axe-sweep.mjs never reads the HTTP status at all. - web/scripts/axe-sweep-authed.mjs prints it and never fails on it. So a route that 404s, or bounces to /login, yields no violations and was counted as clean. This is precisely the mistake caught on the marketing side earlier today, where /trust/ returned 404 and its silence had to be excluded rather than counted — the same defect existed in the platform's own tooling, permanently. New web/scripts/axe-platform-sweep.mjs gates every result behind HTTP 200 + unchanged final path + at least 200 characters of rendered text, reports every impact level, enumerates routes from the filesystem rather than a hand list, and fails closed when zero routes are reached. Auth is a programmatic Supabase password grant — no password typed into a form.

issues.title: A stopped test runner SURVIVED and silently corrupted a second run's counts**
issues.note: Not a product defect — a measurement defect, and it invalidated numbers I had already reported. ### What happened I stopped the web certification runner via the harness to free the tree for edits. The harness stopped the wrapper; the runner itself kept going, marching on through its shards. I then started a second run. Both wrote to the same web-summary.txt and the same web-shardN.json files. Measured evidence, not inference — two vitest processes alive at once, from two different runs: | pid | shard | started | | --- | --- | --- | | 22508 / 6652 | shard 2/6 | 11:31:20 | | 9388 / 22540 | shard 3/6 | 11:31:20 | A single 6-shard run executes one shard at a time. Two shards running concurrently is proof of two runners. ### The symptoms it produced, both of which I nearly reported as real * shard 2 → REAL EXIT 124 (timed out) — under contention, not because of any test. * shard 1 → REAL EXIT 1, while its own JSON reported success: true, 416/416 suites and 1167/1167 tests passing, 0 failed. An exit code contradicting its own report. This is the documented process-pressure signature on this box: contention manufactures failures that name innocent files. Both runs' outputs were discarded — a count produced under contention is not a smaller truth, it is not evidence at all. ### Fix — a single-instance lock in run_web.sh Refuses to start when another runner is live (pid-checked, so a stale lock from a dead pid is taken over rather than blocking forever). Red-proven: a second invocation printed the refusal and returned REAL EXIT 91. ### The lesson worth keeping A harness "stopped" does not mean the child died — already on record for claude.exe, and it applies to any long-running child. Reaping must be verified by *counting surviving processes*, not by trusting the stop. My own reap command then killed its own PowerShell process, because the filter matched a command line containing the pattern it was searching for; the working form excludes $PID and builds the literal by conca

issues.title: ACCT-01 FIXED — the account menu asserted "Free" about ENTITLED organisations
issues.note: The plan pill read plan ?? "free", where plan is the Stripe BILLING tier. Entitlement is a different fact — it lives in product_context, surfaced as subscribedProducts. An org can hold a product with no Stripe plan at all; a manual grant is exactly that shape, and the pill then stated "Free" to a user with full access. The repo already knew. TopbarSlot computes hasEntitlement from subscribedProducts with the comment *"Real product entitlement (product_context slots), NOT the stale plan === 'free' flag"* and feeds it to TrialBanner — one JSX element above the topbar. The account menu was simply never given the same input. isFreeProspect() is literally plan === "free" while its docstring claims "an unentitled prospect" — the doc asserts what the code does not check. Fixed by threading subscribedProducts through TopbarSlot -> Topbar -> TopbarAccountMenu -> UserProfileMenu -> PlanBadge; "Free" is now claimed ONLY when the org holds no product, otherwise the pill names what the org actually has via the central productLabel() (never a hardcoded label). A second, dead defect found in the same component: const isCrowMark = ["solo","team"].includes(p) could never be true — p is always normalisePlanToTier() output, which collapses solo->starter and team->pro and can only return free|starter|pro|portfolio. The CrowMark variant was unreachable. Matched against the canonical ladder instead. tsc --noEmit REAL EXIT 0.

issues.title: href="/" is NOT a dead link — DISPROVEN against production
issues.note: An inspection lane reported marketing-nav.tsx:51 href="/" as a live 404 on 13 marketing pages, reasoning that no root page.tsx exists, redirects.mjs has no / source, and Next's generated AppRoutes union has no "/" member. All three of those observations are true, and the conclusion drawn from them is still wrong. Measured on the live surface, which is the only authority for a routing question: https://app.crowagent.ai/ -> 200 (final: https://app.crowagent.ai/login) https://app.crowagent.ai/login -> 200 (control) / resolves. The redirect lives in middleware/proxy.ts, not in redirects.mjs — which is exactly why a file-based search over route files and the redirects config could not see it. The lesson, and it is the same one this release keeps re-teaching: a search over SOURCE cannot settle a question about BEHAVIOUR. Three correct file-level observations composed into a confident false conclusion. Routing questions get answered with a request. Residual, and it is a UX smell rather than a defect: clicking the CrowAgent logo on a marketing page lands the user on /login rather than a marketing home. Worth a product decision, not a bug fix.

issues.title: /social-value — nav item silently ejects users off-origin, via a redirect CHAIN**
issues.note: CONFIRMED on the live surface, and worse than first reported: https://app.crowagent.ai/social-value -> 308 https://crowagent.ai/products/crowmark (permanent, browser-cached) -> ... https://crowagent.ai/crowmark/ (200) (the destination redirects AGAIN) Three distinct problems in one nav item (marketing-nav.tsx:29, labelled "Bid Suite"): 1. It leaves the origin without warning. A primary marketing-nav item throws the user from app.crowagent.ai to crowagent.ai. 2. The 308 is PERMANENT, so a browser that has followed it once will not re-consult the server. Reversing this decision later does not reach users who already clicked. 3. It is a redirect CHAIN — the 308 target itself redirects. This repo's own route-moves-r250.test.ts forbids chains for internal moves; the rule simply does not reach a cross-origin destination. Dead code behind it: app/(marketing)/social-value/page.tsx and its layout.tsx both EXIST and are permanently unreachable, because next.config redirects run ahead of filesystem routes. Not fixed unilaterally — it is a product decision, not a bug: either "Bid Suite" should point at a real in-app surface (and the 308 be removed), or the redirect is intended and the page files should be DELETED as dead code and the destination pointed straight at crowagent.ai/crowmark/ to collapse the chain. Both are defensible; they differ in what the marketing nav is *for*.

issues.title: Three ORPHAN routes — live, reachable by URL, unreachable by navigation**
issues.note: /knowledge-base, /settings/profile, /settings/company-profile. Verified independently rather than accepted: a raw string count suggested 6 and 4 inbound references respectively, which looked like refutation. Reading them settles it the other way — every single hit is a COMMENT, an i18n catalogue import path, or a telemetry map key. Not one is a navigational link. (Positive control: /settings/webhooks returns 16 hits and is genuinely linked.) This is the "separate prose from identifiers" trap in miniature: the crude count inflates by ~6x and points the wrong way. /settings/company-profile is the notable one — an entire feature directory (src/features/company-profile/) with no route into it. Why nothing caught this: web/__tests__/infra/internal-links-have-routes.test.ts is a well-built gate — 11 link mechanisms, a real comment-stripping state machine, two-directional resolver controls — but it is ONE-DIRECTIONAL. It proves link -> route and never route -> link, so a live route with zero inbound navigation is invisible to it by construction. It also scores a redirect SOURCE that shadows a real route as "alive", which is precisely how R262-D-263 survived. The fix is a reverse guard, and it must REUSE that file's existing link-extraction and comment-stripping logic rather than growing a second, weaker extractor — otherwise the two directions will disagree about what counts as a link, and the disagreement will be silent. Orphans that are deliberate get an EXPIRING, justified allowlist entry (the KNOWN_DEBT pattern in product-label-is-centralised.test.ts, which proved its worth this session by failing the moment its debt was discharged), never a permanent exemption.

issues.title: The "sidebar vanished at 1280px" alarm was an AUTH failure wearing a UI costume**
issues.note: A lane reported responsive-authed.spec.ts "desktop control (1280x900)" failing with *"no sidebar is visible at 1280px … Candidates: none found"*, and attributed it — reasonably — to the concurrent sidebar SSR work, which was mid-flight across the four sidebar-mount files. Measured instead of accepted. Re-running that exact test: 1 failed [setup] › e2e\auth.setup.ts:71:6 › authenticate 1 did not run TimeoutError: waiting for getByRole('navigation', {name: /navigation/i}).first() to be visible The desktop-control test NEVER RAN. The failure is in the auth setup; the sidebar assertion was never reached. "Candidates: none found" is what you get when login does not complete and the page under test is not a dashboard at all — there is no sidebar in it because there is no shell in it. The sidebar is fine, and that is independently evidenced: id="main-sidebar" (sidebar.tsx:643) and data-collapsed (:654) are on the SAME <aside>, and the SSR change proved data-collapsed appears in AUTHENTICATED SERVER HTML tracking the cookie — with a control in which ssr:false was temporarily restored and the marker count dropped to 0. The lesson is the expensive one: an authenticated E2E suite that cannot authenticate does not report "auth failed". It reports domain-shaped failures — missing sidebars, missing nav, empty tables — each of which looks exactly like a real regression in whatever the reader is currently working on. Two lanes nearly filed this against the sidebar refactor. Before believing any authenticated-E2E failure, confirm the SETUP step passed.

issues.title: R262-B-02's money premise is FALSE — measured against live Stripe
issues.note: The phase-4 triage reported, from the tracker, that six live-mode Stripe prices up to £21,589/yr are sellable with zero entitlement code behind them, quoting *"if a private-sector buyer paid £1,999/month today they would receive nothing."* I relayed that as the release's top money risk. No £21,589. No £1,999. Nobody can pay for the buyer tier because there is nothing to pay for. The "money-live / capability-absent" framing is wrong, and B-02 is ordinary unbuilt scope, not a leak. How the false alarm formed, because the shape matters more than the item:** the code-side half was verified correctly (no crowagent_buyer_* key anywhere, with a positive control) — and the Stripe-side half was taken from RELEASE-2.6.2-TRACKER.md. One half measured, one half recorded, and the two composed into a confident conclusion that neither supported alone. A verified absence in the code plus an UNVERIFIED presence in a document is not evidence of a mismatch. This is the same mechanism as the "sidebar vanished" alarm (an auth failure wearing a UI costume) and the href="/" 404 (three correct file observations composing into a wrong conclusion) — three instances in one session of a true premise and a false one being combined. Confirmed in passing, both correct: portfolio_monthly £549 remains an ACTIVE price object with metadata "publish":"never" and the note *"contact-sales only; price must never render on a public surface"* — consistent with R262-D-166, which was cl

issues.title: [EV-04] A pack was four downloads that could disagree with each other
issues.note: The gap was never the renderers — all four existed. It was the signature: generate_proposal_pack took a single fmt and returned ONE file, so a recipient assembling a pack took four separate downloads, minutes apart, each re-reading the contract. Four artefacts describing four different states of the same bid, with nothing able to detect it. generate_proposal_bundle renders every artefact from ONE assembly and stamps a shared SHA-256 digest of the canonical fact set into each artefact and the manifest, so a recipient can VERIFY the files describe the same bid rather than trust that they do. ZIP entries use a fixed mtime, so identical inputs give identical bytes. generate_proposal_pack keeps its old signature and produces byte-identical output for existing callers.

issues.title: [EV-05][RD-07] Four CXO lenses that CANNOT disagree — enforced, not intended
issues.note: CIO/CTO/CFO/COO briefs off one committed fact set. The load-bearing property is that the four lenses can never state different numbers, and it is structural: * a DecisionLens carries fact KEYS and has no numeric field at all; * an import-time guard rejects any lens whose prose contains a digit, so a hardcoded "12% saving" cannot even be imported; * build_decision_facts asserts it produced exactly the declared key set, so a dropped fact fails loudly instead of silently emptying a section; * the fact map is a sealed _FrozenDict — a renderer that "fixes up" a value raises. Anti-invention, and the sharpest case: an unrecorded figure renders "Not recorded: <reason>", never 0. Social-value share is deliberately UNAVAILABLE when contract value is 0, because the pack computes sv_pct = 0.0 there — printing "0% of contract value" to a CFO would state as committed something the record does not contain. A section whose facts are all unrecorded is omitted, and the omission is stated. RED-PROVED, and the first red run is the interesting part: injecting a CFO-only reformat turned 2 of 3 checks red — the cross-artefact check keyed on (item, section) and the two lenses file that item under different section headings, so it passed while diverging. The instrument was fixed to key on the item alone, re-run red (3 failures), then reverted green. *A guard that agrees with the defect is worse than no guard.*

issues.title: [CARRY-13] The judge gate was SKIPPING, and a skipped gate is not a passing gate
issues.note: The panel was wired; the corpus was missing. .github/workflows/eval-gate.yml guarded on if [ -f "$JUDGE_EVAL_SAMPLES" ] and took the else branch on every run since it was written. CI was green because it never ran. Corpus built from verbatim line slices of files already committed here — three real OGL-v3 Contracts Finder tenders plus the bundled citation corpus — each sample carrying an anchor naming file + line range, and criteria quoted verbatim from each tender's own published table. Model non-determinism was ELIMINATED, not bounded, and that is stated rather than hidden. CI sets no API key, so every judge's *opinion* degrades to unavailable and the panel prints INCOMPLETE, never PASS. What gates is the deterministic half of three judges (figure grounding, citation resolution at the shipped 0.92 threshold, criteria coverage). So this is a regression gate on the deterministic engine over real tender contexts — NOT a measurement of model quality, and the README and workflow comment both say so. RED-PROOF: a degraded sample (a fabricated £48,500 appended) → STATUS: FAIL, exit 1, with the other two deterministic judges still passing — the red is targeted, not a blanket failure. Positive control on the committed corpus: 4 samples, 0 failed, exit 0. One trap closed on the way: the recorder rewrites the agent's [TENDER-n] handles to the bare [n] the citation gate reads. Without it every recorded citation is invisible to the gate and the sample passes for the wrong reason — proven by a test.

issues.title: [CARRY-11] Critique loop measured, with its scope stated on the report itself
issues.note: Mean coverage 61.500 -> 78.340 (+16.840) over 5 golden cases: 2 improved, 3 unchanged, 0 degraded. Every number computed by the shipped marker; every keep/discard by the shipped loop under the shipped response gate. The limit is printed in the report so it cannot be quoted out of context: the revision text is REPLAYED from the case file, not generated (no GEMINI_API_KEY in this environment, verified unset). +16.840 measures the LOOP, not the model. Two adversarial controls carry the honesty — a worse revision that must be discarded, and one scoring HIGHER while minting £18,750, where the gate must outrank coverage. The first version of the "worse revision" control was itself broken: its draft sat above the STRONG band, so the loop skipped it and the discard rule never ran — yet it "passed". Fixed, and each case now asserts its loop OUTCOME, not just its delta.

issues.title: [Partner] The console offered what it could not deliver, and locked out the orgs entitled to it
issues.note: /revenue and /branding removed from navigation: a revenue page whose ledger has no writer (its own migration says *"until that exists this ledger stays empty"*), and a branding form persisting settings no exporter reads. issues.title: The dev server leaked ~4GB and was manufacturing failures across every lane
issues.note: Measured, not inferred. The Next dev server grew 2,503 MB -> 3,599 MB -> 4,066 MB over roughly an hour, then to 4,260 MB after a restart; free memory on the 16 GB box fell to 600 MB. This is very likely the common cause behind a day of phantom failures — a lane's dev server "crashing", worker timeouts, "element not found", a shard failing then passing alone. Every one of those was attributed to code at the time. Reclaimed 4,376 MB by closing :3000 and the :8099 board (free 600 -> 4,976 MB). Orphan reaping was measured too and is NOT the lever: three genuinely dead workers returned 28 MB. The long- running server was the whole problem, and it was my own job. Rule going forward: treat a long-lived dev server as a consumable — measure its RSS before blaming a test, and restart it on a schedule rather than when something breaks.

issues.title: CrowMark Buyer is invisible by DESIGN when unentitled — three gates, and CrowMark has none of them
issues.note: Owner report: *"why can't I see CrowMark Buyer's options and pages in the sidebar, which are visible for CrowMark?"* Traced end to end; nothing here is a bug, and that is precisely why it cost time. Three independent gates, all of which must pass: | gate | CrowMark | CrowMark Buyer | | --- | --- | --- | | rail tile (ProductRail.tsx:142) | shown even when UNOWNED (routes to /products?reason=subscription_required) | if (key === "council" && !owned) return [] - hidden entirely | | nav section (nav-config.tsx:594) | unconditional | flagOn && hasPublicSectorAccess(productContext) | | entitlement source | not required to appear | product_context.council.enabled === true | The rail's comment states the intent: *"ALL released products in flagship order, split on entitlement - except Public Sector, which is never advertised to non-council orgs."* Buyer is contact-sales only, so it is deliberately not advertised. The consequence, which is the finding: an unowned CrowMark renders as a VISIBLE UPSELL, while an unowned CrowMark Buyer renders as NOTHING AT ALL - indistinguishable from "this feature does not exist" or "the app is broken". Two products, two opposite failure presentations, and the quieter one belongs to the product a customer is most likely to have been *granted* rather than to have bought. What was actually wrong for this org - BOTH gates failed, not one: 1. council.edition was "off" in staging AND production (set 2026-07-18 / 07-20). Now "on" in both. Note TRUTHY_VALUES = {true,1,on,yes}, so "on" genuinely resolves true - checked before writing rather than after. 2. The owner's org had no council slot at all on staging (has_slot:false). Granted at council_standard, merged via jsonb_set(..., true) so no other product slot was clobbered. Six production orgs already held the entitlement while the flag was off - i.e. six orgs had been granted a product none of them could open. The flag silently outranked the grant. Also measured, and left as a live question rather tha

RULE 0 money audit, same pass: list_deployments on BOTH Vercel projects since the last check returns count 0. Ten local commits remain genuinely unpushed and nothing has been billed. The website ships via Cloudflare from a separate repo, so its production deploy earlier today did not touch the Vercel budget - 3 spent, 1 remaining, unchanged. No blocker exists on any of them.

issues.title: The Products page advertised a price that cannot be charged
issues.note: AddProductsGrid rendered "From £3,600 / year" on the CrowMark Buyer card. All three prices behind that ladder are active:false in live Stripe, archived under PRICING-LOCK-2026-08; two of them because tax_behavior: unspecified is IMMUTABLE and archiving was the only remediation available. Its own header records £8,400/£15,000 placeholders "never created in live Stripe" being shown while Stripe would charge £9,600/£19,200. Centralising on a stale value spreads the stale value. The test was asserting the defect - it pinned /From £3,600 \/ year/, so it would have failed anyone who fixed this. It now asserts the ABSENCE of any £ figure on that card, which survives a re-pricing, with a positive control proving £ figures are findable elsewhere in the same grid.

issues.title: R262-B-01 was STALE, not false - and the distinction is the finding
issues.note: The tracker recorded six live CrowMark Buyer prices on prod_UzhpGUVOh1iups, verified 2026-08-01. A reader took that at face value, concluded six prices were sellable with no entitlement behind them, and reported it as the release's top money risk. I relayed that before measuring. issues.title: Board ID integrity audited after my collision — sound, and my first instrument was wrong
issues.note: Having created one ID collision, the honest next question is whether there are others: the board resolves duplicate ids by LAST-MENTION-WINS, so two DIFFERENT defects sharing an id means one status silently overwrites the other, on the surface every release decision reads from. Result: SOUND. Exactly six ids appear more than once, and every one is the SAME defect written about twice - an OPEN entry followed by its FIXED or re-scoped entry: | id | first | second | | --- | --- | --- | | D-192 | criterion 3 closed | all four criteria met | | D-224 | PPN 002 superseded | PPN 026 confirmed, re-scoped P0 -> P1 | | D-238 | duplicate TOMs measures OPEN | FIXED | | D-239 | no timeout bounds a hanging API test | FIXED | | D-243 | dead lookup-key gate | FIXED | | D-54 | audit env P2 | re-scoped P1 | For these, last-mention-wins is CORRECT rather than a hazard - a defect's latest status should win. My D-249 was the only true collision, and it is resolved (moved to D-282). ### The instrument was wrong first, which is the part worth keeping My initial check scored heading similarity and flagged 5 of the 6 as suspected distinct-defect collisions. All five were false: a row's OPEN title and its FIXED title are worded differently *by design* ("TWO exact duplicate TOMs measures are BOTH ACTIVE" vs "duplicates deactivated, and a duplicate is now impossible"), so low similarity measures PROGRESS, not distinctness. A heuristic that cannot tell a state change from a subject change will report every fixed defect as a collision. Six candidates was small enough to read directly, and reading them took less time than tuning the threshold would have. When the population is small, look at it - do not build an instrument you then have to validate.

The query distinguishes. The same shape produced the "empty set" claim about dunning_state (the table did not exist at all) and the "RD-02/RD-03 have no persistence" claim (it lives in a JSONB column). issues.title: CSP blocks React's streaming runtime in production — $RC is not defined, 32 events on a public page**
issues.note: My filed diagnosis was wrong. I wrote that Next nonces its own scripts but not React's. The real gap: a per-request nonce and a build-time prerendered document are mutually exclusive. Confirmed three ways — react-dom 19.2.5 source (flushCompletedBoundary nonces only when one was supplied to *that* render), next 16.2.6 source (base-server.js has zero nonce references, so a nonce does NOT force dynamic rendering), and a live measurement: the identical script is un-nonced on prerendered routes and nonced on a dynamic route in the same build, same server, same policy. A hash cannot fix it — the runtime chunk shares a tag with per-stream boundary ids, so the digest moves every build. A build-time hash manifest cannot either: middleware is bundled before the export phase that produces the HTML. /sub-processors went 35 inline scripts / 0 nonced / 33 BLOCKED → 31 / 30 / 0. Positive control on the same instrument: /login passed on the very server where /sub-processors failed. COST, and it is the owner's to weigh: cacheComponents:false + force-dynamic are ONE change — with cacheComponents:true Next rejects the export outright and there is no per-route escape hatch. PPR is gone: 456 routes, 3 static. More Vercel invocations, a RULE 0 line item, against a public pre-login page whose content can never render. No policy was weakened. Also: next build was already RED on this tree, at HEAD and at 68909614, failing export on five routes. This change makes it complete — 214/214, the first full production build of the tree.

issues.title: A SECOND theme selector on /settings/privacy saves your choice and never changes the theme**
issues.note: Converged rather than repaired: the card dropped the field, because /settings/appearance already owns theme with previews and an awaitable setPreferredTheme. Third two-writers-one-policy case this release, and the same resolution each time — pick the canonical path and delete the other, never teach the dead one to work. The signpost to Appearance renders outside the loading and error branches, so a failed GET still tells the user where theme lives. Two copy defects one level up were false by inspection and fixed with it. ### The hydrate guard was worse than "a slow control", and its twin was broken too dbTheme !== 'dark' reduces to *"apply the account theme only when it is light"*. Its comment claimed it "only overrides the localStorage default when the DB value differs" — but dark is only the default when localStorage is empty. Once localStorage held light, an account whose stored theme was dark could never pull the browser back: the branch was unreachable for exactly the value that needed it. The currency twin had the identical defect (dbCurrency !== 'gbp') — the fifth "a careful sweep leaves exactly one survivor" of this release. Both fixed. Unconditional application is only safe with precedence, so three rules were added rather than assumed: an in-flight local write beats the account's older value; an explicit system intent outranks the account column (without this, applying unconditionally would have silently downgraded System to a fixed theme on every reload — under the old guard it only bit System users whose OS was light); and currency is validated before use, where the old code cast a raw column value straight into Intl.NumberFormat. Four red-proofs in isolation; on the hydrate one both paired controls kept passing, so the instrument is demonstrably working in both directions.

issues.note: I recorded that production needs deploy-regulatory-corpus run manually "against a live Gemini credential", and set out to check whether I actually had access rather than claim a permission blocker. The access question was the wrong question. scheduler.py compares deployed_regulatory_digest(supabase) against regulatory_corpus_digest(load_regulatory_corpus()), and load_regulatory_corpus() reads the file from the DEPLOYED IMAGE. So pushing the corrected text into production's table today — while the running image still carries the pre-fix file — would be reverted by this very fix at the next scheduler run, which would find a digest mismatch and re-deploy the stale text over it. The correct order is: push → Railway rebuilds with the corrected corpus → the nightly job detects the difference and deploys it automatically. That is the delivery mechanism D-301 exists to create, and using it is better than bypassing it with prod secrets on a workstation. So I did not read the production Gemini key. Checking access was right; the finding is that access was never the constraint. Verify after the push, by object rather than by log: prod content_chunks where source_type='regulatory' should be 172 rows, all embedded (it is 162 today, serving the pre-fix text). Staging remains a separate, real gap unaffected by any of this: ZERO regulatory rows, and 948 tender_document chunks with ZERO embeddings.

issues.title: Three shared primitives use a type scale WEB DOES NOT DECLARE**
issues.note: My own row said the mapping must not be guessed. So I went looking for it, and it already existed. --type-1..12 are declared in packages/tokens/src/tokens.css, which web imports at line 2, and the twelve mapping lines are byte-identical to the ones apps/portal/src/app/globals.css:109-120 has always carried. Nothing was decided; something was connected. Same shape as DS-05, where two type scales existed and nothing joined them. Proven both directions, with a negative control: | class | before | after | | --- | --- | --- | | .text-ca-3 | NOT EMITTED | font-size: var(--text-ca-3) | | .text-sm *(control)* | emitted | emitted | | .text-ca-99 *(negative control)* | — | still NOT EMITTED | The negative control is what makes it conclusive: the compiler emits only *declared* steps, so the positives are not an artefact of the probe. ### The sweep found two more, and those were worse than unstyled .border-ca-border and .border-ca-surf3 also emitted nothing. With no border-color rule, CSS falls back to currentColor — so box.tsx:24 and page-layout.tsx:42 were drawing their borders in the text colour. Not a missing style, a wrong one, on two shared primitives. ### Why it shipped twice in one day, and what now stops it R262-D-302 was the same defect in the var() shape, and the guard written for it could not see this one — it scans var(--x) references, and a Tailwind utility class carries no var(). The guard now carries a second block resolving every (text|bg|border|fill|stroke)-ca-* utility to its namespace (--text-ca-N for the numeric scale, --color-ca-X otherwise) and asserting each is declared, with a negative control on the mapping function itself. Red-proved in a real file. Both populations are now zero — the var() shape and the utility shape. That is what makes both cheap to keep, and it is the difference between a guard and a backlog.

issues.title: The browser tab goes NAMELESS after two quick client-side hops, permanently**
issues.note: ~185 instrumented journeys against a production build. The row I filed was wrong in three ways. ### 1. It is not only the title — and this is the part that raises the stakes On a blank run the entire Next-generated head block is removed and never replaced: charset=false viewport=false description=false og=0, held at readyState: "complete". A missing viewport meta is a mobile-layout defect, so the blast radius is far wider than a nameless tab. The mutation log is unambiguous: the good hop removes the block and re-inserts it in the same tick; the bad hop removes it and inserts nothing. ### 2. The discriminator is the DESTINATION, not the source My row implied the CrowMark pages were special. They are not — the first pass simply never tried the other intermediates. Any two-hop journey landing on /settings degrades: | journey | result | | --- | --- | | /crowmark → opportunities → /settings | 10 BLANK / 12 | | /crowmark → analytics → /settings | 4 BLANK / 8 | | /crowmark → /home → /settings | 3 BLANK / 8 | | /crowmark → /products → /settings | 5 bad / 8 | | four journeys landing elsewhere | 8 clean / 8 each | | single hop to /settings | 11 clean / 12 | So the second hop is required for the blank mode, and /settings is the common factor. ### 3. Three failure modes, not one BLANK, DUPLICATE (two <title> elements) and STALE. One run ended carrying the *entry* route's title, with no charset and no viewport, but the *destination's* description and og tags — so the head is not applied atomically on failure. ### Cause, with a paired control on one instrument | condition | result | | --- | --- | | every Next-Router-Prefetch: 1 request aborted | 0 BLANK / 12 | | unmodified *(control)* | 10 BLANK / 12 | Narrowing does not help: aborting only /settings still gives 4 BLANK/10; simulating prefetch={false} on the settings sidebar gives 5 bad/12; aborting everything *except* /settings gives 0 BLANK/10. The trigger is aggregate prefetch concurrency racing the commit, not one poisoned ca
